Local file: the authors' free personal-use draft copy (ShalevShwartzBenDavid-2014-UnderstandingMachineLearning.pdf), held identically in the library buckets books-must-have and books-d-models; the copy states it is almost, but not entirely, identical to the printed version, with page numbers not identical but section numbers the same. PDF size 2601512 bytes; scan digest sha256(str(size) + file bytes) = 1b3c4e45427fb361fbdfbad0bcecae5959002446ecc1fe71c6518ce1e9cbd6cd; book_id is its first 16 hex chars. Extracted text: 22185 lines, 1247889 characters, complete from Preface through Chapter 31, Appendices, Notes, References, and Index. Text quality: prose extraction is clean and complete; mathematical glyphs are partially degraded (epsilon prints as control character U+000F throughout, the asterisk of h* prints as ?, angle brackets print as h and i), and the extractor occasionally splits a word across a space (for example 'hypoth esis'); all verbatim quotes in this artifact were chosen from clean passages and verified as contiguous normalized substrings of the extracted text file. Motif-lane extraction (MOTIF-TIERB-DRAIN-01) of the same work for sync-cloud reconciliation.

primitives.name: True risk: the error of a prediction rule is the probability of mislabeling a fresh draw from the unknown distribution
primitives.verbatim_quote: We define the error of a classifier to be the probability that it does not predict the correct label on a random data point generated by the aforementioned underlying distribution.
primitives.latex: L_{D,f}(h) = \Pr_{x \sim D}[h(x) \neq f(x)] = D(\{x : h(x) \neq f(x)\})

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_{D,f}(h): true risk (generalization error) of hypothesis h, a probability in [0,1]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.D: unknown probability distribution over the domain X
symbol_and_unit_ledger.h: prediction rule from X to Y

assumptions: The learner is blind to D and f; only the training sample is observable
Examples are drawn i.i.d. from D
primitives.breakdown_regime: Useless without a sample-based proxy: the true risk can never be computed directly, only estimated, so every downstream guarantee is probabilistic.

layer2.mapping: The engine treats every signal family's live accuracy as an unknown true risk: the quantity that matters is performance on future, unseen games drawn from the same process, never performance on the games already seen. Every evaluation layer in the engine is an estimator of this quantity and must carry its sampling uncertainty with it.
layer2.telemetry: Settled outcomes of past predictions versus the predictions issued before those games, logged with timestamps so no future information leaks into the estimate.

primitives.name: Empirical risk: the training error, the fraction of sample points a hypothesis mislabels, is the computable proxy for true risk
primitives.verbatim_quote: A useful notion of error that can be calculated by the learner is the training error - the error the classifier incurs over the training sample:

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_S(h): empirical risk of h on sample S, a fraction in [0,1]

assumptions: The sample is drawn i.i.d. from the same distribution that generates future cases
Labels in the sample are the reference truth for scoring
primitives.breakdown_regime: A small or unrepresentative sample makes the empirical risk a biased, high-variance estimate of the true risk; minimizing it alone invites overfitting.

layer2.mapping: Backtest accuracy is the engine's empirical risk: it is the only performance number directly computable, so the engine computes it exactly and completely, but never promotes a signal on backtest accuracy alone; the gap to live performance is handled by the uniform-convergence and stability machinery elsewhere in this artifact.
layer2.telemetry: Per-signal hit and miss counts over historical games, stored as raw counts so empirical risks can be recomputed for any window or subset.

primitives.name: Empirical Risk Minimization: choose the hypothesis that minimizes empirical risk over the hypothesis class
primitives.verbatim_quote: This learning paradigm - coming up with a predictor h that minimizes LS (h) - is called Empirical Risk Minimization or ERM for short.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.ERM_H(S): the hypothesis returned by ERM over class H on sample S
symbol_and_unit_ledger.argmin: the set of hypotheses in H achieving the minimum empirical risk
symbol_and_unit_ledger.H (script H): hypothesis class fixed before seeing the data

assumptions: The hypothesis class H is chosen in advance, before seeing the training data (the inductive bias)
A minimizer exists or is approximated by the optimizer
primitives.breakdown_regime: Unrestricted ERM overfits (see the memorization counterexample); ERM is only as safe as the class restriction, the sample size, and the optimizer's ability to actually find the minimum.

layer2.mapping: Model fitting inside the engine is ERM with an explicitly declared hypothesis class: each model family (for example a class of weighted signal combinations) is written down before fitting, and the fit is the empirical-risk minimizer inside that class, so later audits can ask exactly which class a number came from.
layer2.telemetry: Training samples per model family, the declared class definition, and the attained empirical risk of the fitted hypothesis.

primitives.name: Overfitting: a memorizing predictor achieves zero training error and true error one half; fit to the sample is not evidence of generalization
primitives.verbatim_quote: We have found a predictor whose performance on the training set is excellent, yet its performance on the true "world" is very poor. This phenomenon is called overfitting.
primitives.latex: h_S(x) = \begin{cases} y_i & \text{if } \exists i \in [m] \text{ s.t. } x_i = x \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

symbol_and_unit_ledger.h_S: the memorizing predictor built from sample S
symbol_and_unit_ledger.y_i: label of the memorized example x_i
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_D(h_S) = 1/2: true error in the book's example, no better than chance

assumptions: The hypothesis class is rich enough to contain a memorizing predictor
The sample is finite, so almost every future point is unseen
primitives.breakdown_regime: The example is a worst-case construction, but the failure mode is generic: any class with enough capacity relative to sample size can interpolate noise.

layer2.mapping: The engine's anti-overfit tripwire: any signal or model whose in-sample fit is dramatically better than its out-of-sample record is treated as a memorizer until proven otherwise, and its weight is cut. Perfect-looking backtests are treated as evidence of leakage or interpolation, not of skill.
layer2.telemetry: In-sample versus out-of-sample performance deltas per model, plus checks for duplicated or near-duplicated historical cases that a memorizer could exploit.

primitives.name: Realizability assumption: some hypothesis in the class labels the world perfectly, so zero true risk is attainable inside the class
primitives.verbatim_quote: definition 2.1 (The Realizability Assumption) There exists h? ∈ H s.t.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.h*: a perfect hypothesis inside H (printed as h? in the extracted text)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_{(D,f)}(h*): true risk of h*, equal to zero under the assumption

assumptions: Labels are a deterministic function of the features the learner can see
The perfect rule lies inside the chosen hypothesis class
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails whenever labels are stochastic given the observed features, which is the normal case in real domains; the agnostic model of Chapter 3 is the repair.

layer2.mapping: The engine never assumes a perfect rule exists for a game outcome: outcomes are stochastic given every observable feature set, so realizability is used only as a diagnostic fiction. If a fitted model behaves as if a perfect separator existed, that is flagged as a data problem, not a discovery.
layer2.telemetry: Label-noise estimates: rates at which near-identical historical situations produced different outcomes.

primitives.name: Finite classes are learnable: ERM over a finite class does not overfit once the sample exceeds log of class size over accuracy
primitives.verbatim_quote: In this section, we show that if H is a finite class then ERMH will not overfit, provided it is based on a sufficiently large training sample (this size requirement will depend on the size of H).
primitives.page: Chapter 2, Section 2.3.1 and Corollary 2.3 (p. 37-41); text lines ~1340-1490

symbol_and_unit_ledger.m: required sample size, count of examples
symbol_and_unit_ledger.|H|: number of hypotheses in the finite class
symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon: target accuracy, excess true risk bound

assumptions: Realizability holds for the clean version of the bound
Examples are i.i.d.
The union bound over all bad hypotheses is the proof mechanism
primitives.breakdown_regime: The bound is usually loose (union bound ignores correlations between hypotheses) and the log-size scaling breaks down for infinite classes, which need VC-dimension or Rademacher complexity instead.

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's minimum-evidence rule for discrete model zoos: if the engine searches over N candidate configurations, the sample of settled games required before trusting the best one grows with log N. Configuration search budgets are therefore logged and charged against the evidence requirement.
layer2.telemetry: Counts of candidate configurations actually tried per model family, and settled-game counts per family, so the log-size evidence charge can be computed.

primitives.name: PAC learnability: a class is learnable if some algorithm, from a distribution-free number of examples, returns a hypothesis that is probably approximately correct
primitives.verbatim_quote: definition 3.1 (PAC Learnability) A hypothesis class H is PAC learnable if there exist a function mH : (0, 1)2 → N and a learning algorithm with the following property:

symbol_and_unit_ledger.m_H(epsilon, delta): sample complexity: examples needed for accuracy epsilon at confidence 1 - delta

assumptions: The guarantee must hold for every distribution D and every labeling function f (distribution-free)
Realizability holds in the basic version
primitives.breakdown_regime: Distribution-free guarantees are conservative: they price in adversarial distributions that never occur in practice, so PAC sample sizes overstate what a specific domain needs.

layer2.mapping: The engine adopts the PAC contract shape for every promoted signal: a stated accuracy target, a stated confidence, and a required sample size, all fixed before the evaluation runs. A signal that cannot state its (epsilon, delta, m) triple is not promotable, whatever its backtest looks like.
layer2.telemetry: Pre-registered evaluation specs per signal: target edge, confidence level, and the number of settled games the evaluation will use.

primitives.name: Agnostic PAC learnability: without realizability, success means coming within epsilon of the best hypothesis in the benchmark class
primitives.verbatim_quote: definition 3.3 (Agnostic PAC Learnability) A hypothesis class H is agnostic PAC learnable if there exist a function mH : (0, 1)2 → N and a learning algorithm with the following property:

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_D(h): true risk under a joint distribution D over X x Y (labels may be stochastic)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.min over h' in H: risk of the best benchmark hypothesis in the class
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_D: the Bayes optimal predictor, the pointwise majority label rule, which lower-bounds every classifier's risk

assumptions: Labels come from a joint distribution over instances and labels, so the Bayes risk may be positive
The benchmark is relative: the learner competes with the class, not with perfection
primitives.breakdown_regime: If the benchmark class is poor, agnostic success is weak: beating the best in a bad class can still be bad in absolute terms.

layer2.mapping: Engine evaluation is agnostic by design: a signal is scored against the best achievable benchmark for its market (for example the closing consensus as the benchmark class's best member), and credited only for excess performance over that benchmark, never for raw accuracy in a noisy domain.
layer2.telemetry: Benchmark performance series (consensus or market baseline) aligned game by game with each signal's predictions.

primitives.name: Uniform convergence: if empirical risks approximate true risks uniformly over the whole class, ERM is guaranteed to generalize
primitives.verbatim_quote: For that, it suffices to ensure that the empirical risks of all members of H are good approximations of their true risk. Put another way, we need that uniformly over all hypotheses in the hypothesis class, the empirical risk will be close to the true risk, as formalized in the following.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon-representative sample: a sample S whose empirical risks are all within epsilon of the true risks (Definition 4.1)

assumptions: The bound must hold simultaneously for all hypotheses, including data-dependent ones like the ERM output
Concentration (Hoeffding-type) plus a union or covering argument supplies the probability
primitives.breakdown_regime: Uniform convergence is sufficient but not necessary for learnability, and worst-case uniform bounds can be vacuous for very rich classes even when learning succeeds in practice.

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's multiple-testing discipline stated as mathematics: because the engine selects signals after seeing their backtests, the selection is only trustworthy if the backtest-to-live gap is controlled uniformly over everything that was tried, not just over the winner. Evaluation reports therefore bound the gap for the whole candidate pool at once.
layer2.telemetry: The full candidate pool per evaluation (including rejected signals), per-candidate backtest errors, and the pool size used in the uniform bound.

primitives.name: No-Free-Lunch theorem: for every learner there is a task it fails on which another learner solves; there is no universal learner
primitives.verbatim_quote: This theorem states that for every learner, there exists a task on which it fails, even though that task can be successfully learned by another learner.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.m < |X|/2: training set smaller than half the domain
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_D(A(S)) >= 1/8: the algorithm's true risk on the adversarial task, while some f in the class has risk 0

assumptions: The adversarial distribution is chosen after seeing the algorithm
The domain is large relative to the sample
primitives.breakdown_regime: The theorem is about worst cases over all distributions; it does not say learning fails on the distributions a given domain actually generates. Prior knowledge is exactly what escapes it.

layer2.mapping: The engine assumes no signal family is universal: every family has regimes where it fails, so the reasoning layer must carry per-family regime tags rather than global trust. A claim that a new method works everywhere is treated as a claim that it works nowhere in particular.
layer2.telemetry: Per-family performance broken down by regime descriptors (league, season phase, game context) to locate each family's failure regions.

primitives.name: Error decomposition: total risk splits into approximation error (bias of the class) plus estimation error (price of fitting a finite sample)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The Estimation Error - the difference between the approximation error and the error achieved by the ERM predictor. The estimation error results because the empirical risk (i.e., training error) is only an estimate of the true risk

symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon_app: approximation error: best true risk inside the class; grows as the class shrinks
symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon_est: estimation error: excess risk from fitting a finite sample; grows with class complexity, shrinks with m

assumptions: The decomposition is exact by definition; the tradeoff appears because enlarging H moves the two terms in opposite directions
Estimation error bounds come from uniform convergence over H
primitives.breakdown_regime: The two terms are not separately observable in practice; both must be inferred from validation behavior, and the split can mislead if the class is misspecified in ways the sample cannot reveal.

layer2.mapping: Every engine postmortem splits a model's shortfall into the two named parts: was the model family incapable of expressing the pattern (approximation), or did it fit noise in the available games (estimation)? The fix differs completely, more features and richer families for the first, more data and stronger regularization for the second, so the split is recorded for every material miss.
layer2.telemetry: Learning-curve measurements: performance as a function of training-window size, which separates a flat approximation floor from a still-falling estimation term.

primitives.name: VC-dimension: the size of the largest set a class can shatter; the combinatorial capacity that characterizes learnability
primitives.verbatim_quote: definition 6.5 (VC-dimension) The VC-dimension of a hypothesis class H, denoted VCdim(H), is the maximal size of a set C ⊂ X that can be shattered by H.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.H_C: restriction of H to the finite set C: all labelings of C that H can realize
symbol_and_unit_ledger.shattering: H realizes every one of the 2^|C| labelings of C
symbol_and_unit_ledger.VCdim(H): maximal |C| that H shatters; infinite if arbitrarily large sets are shattered

assumptions: Defined for binary-valued classes
Shattering is about existence of one hard set, not typical sets
primitives.breakdown_regime: VC-dimension ignores the distribution and the geometry of typical data, so it can badly overstate the effective capacity on real domains; it also does not directly measure regression or multiclass capacity (those need other dimensions).

layer2.mapping: The engine uses VC-style capacity accounting as a ceiling on model ambition: a model family whose effective capacity approaches the number of settled games available cannot be validated, so capacity budgets (features, interactions, free parameters) are set from sample size first, and model design works inside the budget.
layer2.telemetry: Effective capacity proxies per model (parameter counts, feature counts, interaction depth) logged next to available sample sizes at fit time.

primitives.name: Fundamental theorem of statistical learning: uniform convergence, ERM success, PAC learnability, and finite VC-dimension are all equivalent, and VC-dimension sets the sample complexity
primitives.verbatim_quote: theorem 6.7 (The Fundamental Theorem of Statistical Learning) Let H be a hypothesis class of functions from a domain X to {0, 1} and let the loss function be the 0 − 1 loss. Then, the following are equivalent:
assumptions: Binary classification with the 0-1 loss
The quantitative version (Theorem 6.8) gives sample complexity Theta((d + log(1/delta))/epsilon^2) in the agnostic case for VC-dimension d
primitives.breakdown_regime: The equivalence is for binary classification; other tasks (multiclass, regression, online) need their own characterizations, and the constants in the quantitative version are not sharp enough for direct engineering use.

layer2.mapping: This theorem is the engine's constitution for classification-style signals: if a signal family's capacity is finite and controlled, ERM-style fitting plus enough settled games is a complete justification chain; if capacity is uncontrolled, no amount of backtesting repairs it. Architecture reviews cite which leg of the equivalence a new component relies on.
layer2.telemetry: Capacity estimates and settled-sample counts per signal family, reviewed whenever a family is added or enlarged.

primitives.name: Structural Risk Minimization: order hypotheses by a prior weighting over nested classes and minimize empirical risk plus the class's generalization penalty
primitives.verbatim_quote: The SRM rule follows a "bound minimization" approach. This means that the goal of the paradigm is to find a hypothesis that minimizes a certain upper bound on the true risk.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.n(h): index of the smallest class H_n containing h
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w(n): prior weight of class H_n, weights sum to at most 1
symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon_n(m, delta): uniform-convergence gap for class H_n at sample size m

assumptions: H is a countable union of classes each enjoying uniform convergence
The weight function encodes prior preference and must be fixed before seeing data
primitives.breakdown_regime: Poorly chosen weights waste the guarantee on implausible classes; the bound minimized is an upper bound, so SRM can be conservative relative to the actual risks.

layer2.mapping: The engine's model-selection rule is SRM in structure: candidate models live in explicitly nested tiers (simple signal averages, then interaction models, then rich ensembles), each tier carries a prior weight, and selection minimizes backtest error plus the tier's penalty term rather than backtest error alone.
layer2.telemetry: Tier assignments and prior weights per model family, the penalty term computed for each candidate at selection time, and the selected bound value.

primitives.name: Minimum Description Length and Occam's razor: a hypothesis with a shorter description earns a tighter generalization bound at the same empirical risk
primitives.verbatim_quote: It follows that in this case, the prior knowledge is solely determined by the weight we assign to each hypothesis. We assign higher weights to hypotheses that we believe are more likely to be the correct one

symbol_and_unit_ledger.|h|: length in bits of the description of h in a fixed prefix-free language
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w(h) = 2^{-|h|}: the weight induced by the description length via Kraft's inequality

assumptions: The description language is fixed before seeing data and is prefix-free
H is countable
primitives.breakdown_regime: Description length is language-relative: a hypothesis that is short in one encoding is long in another, so MDL conclusions inherit the arbitrariness of the chosen language; the bound also loosens for hypotheses whose descriptions are long but structured.

layer2.mapping: The engine prices model complexity in description terms: a candidate pattern that takes many bits to state (many conditions, exceptions, and tuned thresholds) must buy its bound with proportionally more settled games than a pattern statable in one line. Pattern proposals are written down literally, so their description length is auditable.
layer2.telemetry: The literal written specification of each candidate pattern or rule, retained with its evaluation, so complexity is measured on the statement and not on intuition.

primitives.name: Perceptron: on separable data the online update rule halts after at most (RB)^2 mistakes, a bound independent of dimension and sample size
primitives.verbatim_quote: theorem 9.1 Assume that (x1 , y1 ), . . . , (xm , ym ) is separable, let B = min{kwk : ∀i ∈ [m], yi hw, xi i ≥ 1}, and let R = maxi kxi k.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.T: number of Perceptron iterations (mistakes) before halting
symbol_and_unit_ledger.B: norm of the smallest separator achieving margin 1 on every example
symbol_and_unit_ledger.R: largest norm of any training instance

assumptions: The data is separable by a halfspace through the origin (homogeneous case as stated)
Labels are in {+1, -1} and instances are real vectors
primitives.breakdown_regime: Separability is essential: on nonseparable data the Perceptron need not converge at all, and the bound says nothing about generalization to new distributions beyond the margin connection developed later.

layer2.mapping: The (RB)^2 form is the engine's template for margin-based trust: what matters is the ratio between the separator's required norm and the data radius, not the raw feature count. Linear signal combiners in the engine report their achieved margin-to-radius ratio, and combiners needing huge norm to fit are distrusted even with perfect fit.
layer2.telemetry: Weight-vector norms and maximum instance norms for each fitted linear combiner, computed at fit time.

primitives.name: Least squares: ERM for linear regression under squared loss reduces to the normal equations Aw = b
primitives.verbatim_quote: To solve the problem we calculate the gradient of the objective function and compare it to zero.
primitives.latex: A w = b, \qquad A = \sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i x_i^\top, \quad b = \sum_{i=1}^{m} y_i x_i

symbol_and_unit_ledger.A: m-fold sum of instance outer products, a d by d matrix
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w: coefficient vector solving the ERM problem for squared loss

assumptions: Squared loss and a linear (homogeneous) predictor class
The objective is convex, so the zero-gradient condition is sufficient as well as necessary
primitives.breakdown_regime: Squared loss is outlier-sensitive and the normal equations are ill-conditioned when features are collinear; A may be singular, in which case the ERM solution is not unique without regularization.

layer2.mapping: Closed-form least squares is the engine's baseline fitter for continuous targets such as projected scores and margins: it is the reference implementation every fancier regressor must beat, and its normal-equation conditioning is reported so collinear signal sets are caught early.
layer2.telemetry: Design-matrix condition numbers and the closed-form solution's out-of-sample error for each regression target.

primitives.name: AdaBoost: reweighting examples toward current mistakes turns a weak learner into a strong one, with training error decaying exponentially in rounds
primitives.verbatim_quote: The following theorem shows that the training error of the output hypothesis decreases exponentially fast with the number of boosting rounds.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.gamma: weak-learning edge: each round's hypothesis has weighted error at most 1/2 - gamma (Definition 10.1)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.h_s: the output weighted-majority classifier, sign of the weighted sum of round hypotheses
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w_t = (1/2) log(1/epsilon_t - 1): round weight from round error epsilon_t

assumptions: A gamma-weak-learner for the base class exists and succeeds at every round, under every reweighting of the sample
Labels in {+1, -1}
primitives.breakdown_regime: The exponential bound is on training error only; generalization needs the margin and VC analysis of combinations, and AdaBoost can overfit noisy labels by concentrating weight on mislabeled examples.

layer2.mapping: The engine's ensemble combiner follows the AdaBoost discipline literally: successive model generations are trained on reweighted histories that emphasize the games the current ensemble gets wrong, and round weights are set from measured round errors rather than tuned by hand.
layer2.telemetry: Per-round weighted errors and assigned weights for each ensemble generation, plus the ensemble's margin distribution on settled games.

primitives.name: Validation: a fresh holdout set estimates true risk with an error bound that depends only on holdout size, not on how the predictor was built
primitives.verbatim_quote: The bound in Theorem 11.1 does not depend on the algorithm or the training set used to construct h and is tighter than the usual bounds that we have seen so far.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_V(h): empirical risk on the validation set V
symbol_and_unit_ledger.m_v: number of fresh validation examples, independent of the training set
symbol_and_unit_ledger.loss in [0,1]: bounded loss is required for this Hoeffding form

assumptions: The validation set is sampled from D independently of everything used to construct h
h is fixed before the validation set is examined (repeated peeking reintroduces selection bias, handled by union bounds or fresh sets)
primitives.breakdown_regime: The bound is per-predictor; selecting the best of many predictors on the same holdout consumes the holdout, which is why train-validation-test discipline exists.

layer2.mapping: Holdout discipline in the engine follows this theorem's logic exactly: a settled-games window that was never used in fitting or selection gives an algorithm-independent error estimate, and the moment it is used for selection it is downgraded to training data and a fresher window is required for the next honest estimate.
layer2.telemetry: Window provenance records: which game windows were used for fitting, for selection, and untouched for final estimation, per model version.

primitives.name: Convexity: a function lies below its chords, which makes local minima global and learning problems tractable
primitives.verbatim_quote: definition 12.2 (Convex Function) Let C be a convex set. A function f : C → R is convex if for every u, v ∈ C and α ∈ [0, 1],

symbol_and_unit_ledger.u, v: points in the convex set C
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f(alpha u + (1-alpha) v): function value at the interpolated point, bounded by the interpolated values

assumptions: C is a convex set (closed under line segments, Definition 12.1)
First-order condition: a differentiable convex f lies above its tangents, f(v) >= f(w) + grad f(w).(v - w)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Most real objectives (neural networks, exact 0-1 loss) are not convex; convexity is bought by changing the loss (surrogates) or the model, and the purchase can change what is being optimized.

layer2.mapping: Wherever the engine can choose its fitting objective, it chooses a convex one: convex subproblems have reproducible, initialization-independent solutions, which makes engine outputs auditable and stable across retrains. Nonconvex fits are quarantined behind extra validation because their solutions depend on the optimizer's path.
layer2.telemetry: Solver diagnostics per fit: attained objective, duality or gradient-norm residuals, and variance of solutions across restarts for nonconvex fits.

primitives.name: Lipschitzness: a rho-Lipschitz function changes at most proportionally to its input, bounding gradients and stabilizing optimization and generalization
primitives.verbatim_quote: definition 12.6 (Lipschitzness) Let C ⊂ Rd . A function f : Rd → Rk is ρ-Lipschitz over C if for every w1 , w2 ∈ C we have that kf (w1 ) − f (w2 )k ≤ ρ kw1 − w2 k.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho: Lipschitz constant: maximum rate of change of f per unit input change
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w1, w2: points in C, subset of R^d
symbol_and_unit_ledger.norm: Euclidean norm unless otherwise stated; for differentiable f, rho bounds the gradient norm

assumptions: Companion notion in the same section: beta-smoothness, the gradient itself is beta-Lipschitz (Definition 12.8), giving the quadratic upper bound used in descent analyses
primitives.breakdown_regime: A global Lipschitz constant can be enormous or infinite for innocent-looking losses on unbounded domains, making the resulting bounds vacuous; local or data-dependent versions are then needed.

layer2.mapping: The engine bounds how fast any model's output may move when one input signal moves: components with effectively unbounded sensitivity to a single input are treated as fragile, because one bad data point can swing the prediction. Sensitivity audits compute empirical Lipschitz-style ratios for each model on historical inputs.
layer2.telemetry: Maximum output change per unit input change per model, measured over historical game feature vectors, with the worst-case input identified.

primitives.name: Surrogate loss: replace a nonconvex target loss by a convex upper bound (hinge for 0-1) so ERM becomes tractable while still controlling the true objective
primitives.verbatim_quote: To circumvent the hardness result, one popular approach is to upper bound the nonconvex loss function by a convex surrogate loss function.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.ell_hinge: hinge loss of halfspace w on example (x, y)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.<w, x>: the halfspace's score; the surrogate requirement is ell_01 <= ell_hinge pointwise

assumptions: The surrogate must be convex and must upper bound the original loss
Minimizing the surrogate is a proxy: consistency (surrogate minimizer also minimizes the target) needs separate verification, as with the logistic loss in Chapter 9
primitives.breakdown_regime: A loose surrogate can be minimized by hypotheses with poor target loss; the gap between surrogate risk and 0-1 risk is exactly the ramp/margin analysis of Chapter 15.

layer2.mapping: Engine objectives are surrogates by the same logic: the quantity actually cared about (did the prediction beat the benchmark) is discontinuous, so fitting uses smooth convex stand-ins such as logistic or hinge-style losses on margins, chosen because they upper bound or calibrate to the real scoring rule.
layer2.telemetry: The exact surrogate used per model, recorded with the fit, plus the target-metric value of the surrogate-optimal model so surrogate-target gaps stay visible.

primitives.name: Regularized Loss Minimization: minimize empirical risk plus a complexity penalty, with Tikhonov (squared norm) as the canonical stabilizer
primitives.verbatim_quote: Formally, a regularization function is a mapping R : Rd → R, and the regularized loss minimization rule outputs a hypothesis in

symbol_and_unit_ledger.lambda > 0: tradeoff scalar between fit and complexity
symbol_and_unit_ledger.||w||^2: squared Euclidean norm in the Tikhonov case (Equation 13.2)

assumptions: The regularizer encodes prior belief about which hypotheses are plausible, exactly as SRM weights and MDL lengths do
The penalty path is traced by varying lambda
primitives.breakdown_regime: Too much regularization underfits (the penalty dominates and the data is ignored); too little returns plain ERM and its overfitting; lambda itself must be selected without corrupting the evaluation.

layer2.mapping: Every fitted combiner in the engine carries an explicit penalty term rather than fitting raw: weights are shrunk toward prior values by a stated lambda, and the lambda is part of the model's identity, so two models differing only in shrinkage are different models with different track records.
layer2.telemetry: Lambda values and penalty magnitudes per fitted model, logged with the unpenalized fit for comparison.

primitives.name: Stability theorem: a learning algorithm's expected generalization gap equals its replace-one instability, so stable rules do not overfit
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 13.2 tells us that a learning algorithm does not overfit if and only if it is on-average-replace-one-stable.
primitives.page: Chapter 13, Section 13.2, Theorem 13.2 and Definition 13.3 (p. 173-174); text lines 7960-8030

symbol_and_unit_ledger.S^{(i)}: training set S with example i replaced by a fresh example z'
symbol_and_unit_ledger.A(S): hypothesis output by algorithm A on S
symbol_and_unit_ledger.epsilon(m): stability rate: the expected loss change from replacing one example, required to shrink with m

assumptions: Expectations are over i.i.d. draws; the identity in Theorem 13.2 is exact, not a bound
Usefulness requires the stability rate epsilon(m) to decrease with sample size, which Tikhonov regularization supplies for Lipschitz or smooth losses
primitives.breakdown_regime: Stability controls only the gap, not the fit: a constant algorithm is perfectly stable and perfectly useless, so stability must be paired with low empirical risk (the fitting-stability tradeoff of Section 13.4).

layer2.mapping: The engine runs replace-one audits on its models: refit with single historical games swapped out and measure prediction movement. Models whose outputs swing on single games are deemed unstable and are shrunk or rejected regardless of headline accuracy, because Theorem 13.2 equates that swing with the expected live-vs-backtest gap.
layer2.telemetry: Replace-one prediction deltas per model over sampled historical games, summarized as mean and tail statistics.

primitives.name: Stochastic Gradient Descent: noisy unbiased gradient steps with averaging reach the GD rate B rho over root T for convex Lipschitz problems
primitives.verbatim_quote: theorem 14.8 Let B, ρ > 0. Let f be a convex function and let w? ∈ argminw:kwk≤B f (w).
primitives.page: Chapter 14, Sections 14.1-14.3, Theorem 14.8 and Corollary 14.2 (p. 185-192); text lines 8533-8975

symbol_and_unit_ledger.B: radius bound on the comparator w* (printed w? in the text)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w-bar: the averaged iterate, the algorithm's output
symbol_and_unit_ledger.eta = (B/rho) sqrt(2/T) scale: step size achieving the stated rate in Theorem 14.8

assumptions: f is convex; stochastic gradients are unbiased with norm at most rho with probability 1
The guarantee is in expectation over the gradient noise
primitives.breakdown_regime: The 1/root-T rate is slow and the bound degrades with rho and B; nonsmooth or nonconvex objectives lose the guarantee, and last-iterate outputs need separate analysis (strong convexity improves the rate, Section 14.4.4).

layer2.mapping: Engine refits on streaming game data use SGD-style updates with iterate averaging for the convex subproblems, and the B rho / root T formula sets expectations: halving optimization error needs four times the games processed, which schedules how often full refits are worth running.
layer2.telemetry: Iteration counts, step sizes, and averaged-versus-last iterate gaps for each production fit.

primitives.name: Margin and Hard-SVM: among all separating hyperplanes, choose the one maximizing the minimal distance to the training points
primitives.verbatim_quote: Hard-SVM is the learning rule in which we return an ERM hyperplane that separates the training set with the largest possible margin.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.margin: minimal distance from any training point to the hyperplane (Claim 15.1: the distance is |<w, x> + b| when ||w|| = 1)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.separability: all constraints y_i(<w, x_i> + b) > 0 hold

assumptions: The training set is linearly separable
The equivalent norm-minimization form (minimize ||w|| subject to y_i(<w,x_i> + b) >= 1) is used in practice
primitives.breakdown_regime: Hard-SVM has no solution on nonseparable data and is sensitive to label noise and outliers near the boundary; sample complexity improves with margin but the approximation error is measured against margin violations (the ramp loss discussion).

layer2.mapping: Margin thinking governs the engine's confidence language: a prediction whose supporting evidence sits far from the decision boundary (large margin in signal space) is issued with higher confidence than one balanced on the boundary, and confidence is computed from the actual distance, not from the model's self-report.
layer2.telemetry: Signed distances of each issued prediction to its decision boundary, retained with the prediction record.

primitives.name: Soft-SVM: trading norm against hinge loss via slack variables is exactly regularized loss minimization with the hinge surrogate
primitives.verbatim_quote: We therefore see that Soft-SVM falls into the paradigm of regularized loss minimization that we studied in the previous chapter.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.xi_i (slack): per-example margin violation in the primal form (Equation 15.4); at the optimum xi_i equals the hinge loss of example i
symbol_and_unit_ledger.lambda: price of norm relative to average hinge loss
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_S^hinge: average hinge loss over the training set

assumptions: Claim 15.5's equivalence: minimizing over the slacks reproduces the hinge loss exactly
The homogeneous variant sets the bias b = 0 (Equation 15.6)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Soft-SVM inherits the surrogate gap: hinge-optimal is not 0-1-optimal, and lambda trades margin width against training violations with no universal setting.

layer2.mapping: The engine's default classifier shape is the Soft-SVM form: a norm penalty plus an average margin-sensitive loss. This is the reference implementation for turning a weighted signal vector into a pick/no-pick decision with an explicit price on model size.
layer2.telemetry: Lambda, attained norm, and hinge-loss totals for each production classifier fit.

primitives.name: Kernel trick: algorithms needing only inner products can work in an implicit feature space through K(x, x') = <psi(x), psi(x')>
primitives.verbatim_quote: Given an embedding ψ of some domain space X into some Hilbert space, we define the kernel function K(x, x0 ) = hψ(x), ψ(x0 )i.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.psi: embedding of X into a Hilbert space (feature space)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.K: kernel function: similarity between instances realized as an inner product
symbol_and_unit_ledger.representer structure: for the regularized problems of Equation (16.2), an optimal w lies in the span of the embedded training points

assumptions: K must be a valid kernel (positive semidefinite Gram matrices; characterization in Section 16.2.2)
The algorithm must access the embedding only through inner products
primitives.breakdown_regime: The Gram matrix costs m^2 memory and the method scales poorly to very large samples; a misspecified kernel encodes the wrong similarity and no optimization repairs it.

layer2.mapping: Similarity between games is the engine's kernel: historical situations are compared through a stated similarity function, and retrieval of analogous past games for a new matchup is kernel evaluation. The similarity definition is versioned like code, because changing it changes every downstream judgment.
layer2.telemetry: Pairwise similarity scores between the target game and retrieved historical games, with the kernel version identifier attached to each reasoning record.

primitives.name: Regret: in online learning, performance is measured against the best fixed hypothesis in hindsight, and the goal is sublinear regret
primitives.verbatim_quote: This is captured by the regret of the algorithm, which measures how "sorry" the learner is, in retrospect, not to have followed the predictions of some hypothesis h ∈ H.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Regret_A(h, T): algorithm's total loss over T rounds minus h's total loss on the same sequence (Equation 21.1)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sup over sequences: the definition takes the worst case over example sequences
symbol_and_unit_ledger.sublinear regret: Regret/T goes to 0, so average performance approaches the best fixed hypothesis

assumptions: No distributional assumption: the sequence may be adversarial
The comparator is the best fixed hypothesis in hindsight, not the best adaptive strategy
primitives.breakdown_regime: Competing with a fixed hypothesis is weak when the environment itself shifts; dynamic comparators need different machinery, and worst-case sequence guarantees can be pessimistic for stochastic environments.

layer2.mapping: The engine keeps a running regret ledger for its live signals against the best fixed alternative in hindsight (for example always following the strongest single signal family). A signal whose cumulative regret grows linearly is retired by rule, because sublinear regret is the minimum bar for an adaptive component.
layer2.telemetry: Cumulative loss series per live signal and per fixed comparator, updated as games settle.

primitives.name: Weighted-Majority: exponentially reweighting experts by their costs achieves regret at most sqrt(2 log d times T) against the best expert
primitives.verbatim_quote: The proof of Theorem 21.10 relies on the Weighted-Majority algorithm for learning with expert advice.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.v_t: cost vector at round t, entries in [0, 1]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.w^{(t)}: the algorithm's distribution over experts at round t
symbol_and_unit_ledger.eta = sqrt(2 log(d)/T) scale: learning rate in the algorithm box

assumptions: Costs are bounded in [0, 1]
The horizon T is given (the doubling trick removes this, per the chapter's exercise note)
primitives.breakdown_regime: The bound is against the single best expert; a rotating cast of regime-specific experts can beat every fixed one, and the sqrt(T) regret is the price of not knowing which expert is best.

layer2.mapping: The engine's signal-weighting layer is a Weighted-Majority instance: each signal family is an expert, weights decay exponentially with realized cost, and the combined prediction is the weighted vote. The log(d) dependence is why adding mediocre families is cheap but not free, and family admission decisions cite it.
layer2.telemetry: Expert weight trajectories per family across the season, with realized per-round costs.

primitives.name: k-means objective: partition the data to minimize total squared distance to cluster centroids, with centroids as cluster means
primitives.verbatim_quote: The k-means objective function measures the squared distance between each point in X to the centroid of its cluster.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C_1..C_k: the partition of X into k clusters
symbol_and_unit_ledger.mu_i(C_i): centroid of cluster i: the point minimizing total squared distance to cluster members
symbol_and_unit_ledger.d: distance in the ambient metric space containing X

assumptions: The number of clusters k is an input, not learned
Squared Euclidean-style distortion is the chosen geometry
primitives.breakdown_regime: The objective is NP-hard to optimize exactly and the standard Lloyd-style algorithm finds local optima; results depend on initialization and on k, and squared distance makes clusters spherical and outlier-sensitive.

layer2.mapping: Situation clustering in the engine (grouping historical games into comparable spots) uses the cost-minimization framing: a clustering is judged by its explicit distortion objective, and alternative groupings compete on measured cost rather than on narrative plausibility.
layer2.telemetry: Distortion totals for the production situation clustering and for challenger clusterings, computed on the same historical game set.

primitives.name: Principal Component Analysis: the linear compression-recovery pair minimizing total squared reconstruction error, solved by the top eigenvectors of the scatter matrix
primitives.verbatim_quote: In PCA, we find the compression matrix W and the recovering matrix U so that the total squared distance between the original and recovered vectors is minimal
primitives.latex: \arg\min_{W \in \mathbb{R}^{n, d}, \, U \in \mathbb{R}^{d, n}} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \|x_i - U W x_i\|_2^2

symbol_and_unit_ledger.W: compression matrix into R^n, n < d
symbol_and_unit_ledger.U: recovery matrix back into R^d; at the optimum its columns are orthonormal and W = U^T (Lemma 23.1)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.A = sum_i x_i x_i^T: scatter matrix whose top eigenvectors give the optimal U (Equation 23.4 form)

assumptions: Linear compression and linear recovery
Squared reconstruction error is the fidelity criterion
primitives.breakdown_regime: PCA keeps high-variance directions, which need not be the informative ones; it is a compression method, and the chapter contrasts it with compressed sensing, whose prior is sparsity rather than variance concentration.

layer2.mapping: Engine feature compression follows the PCA contract when used: the retained subspace is chosen by measured reconstruction error on historical features, and the discarded reconstruction error is reported as a known information loss attached to any model consuming the compressed features.
layer2.telemetry: Reconstruction error per retained dimension for each compressed feature block, with the chosen cutoff recorded.

primitives.name: Maximum Likelihood Estimation: choose the parameter maximizing the (log) likelihood of the observed sample
primitives.verbatim_quote: We define the log likelihood of S, given the parameter θ, as the log of the preceding expression:

symbol_and_unit_ledger.L(S; theta): log likelihood of sample S under parameter theta (the book's script L)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Bernoulli example: for survival indicators the MLE is the sample mean, Equation (24.1), with Hoeffding error sqrt(log(2/delta)/(2m))

assumptions: The model family is specified in advance; MLE is ERM with the log-loss under the model's own distribution (Section 24.1.2)
Examples are i.i.d. under the modeled distribution
primitives.breakdown_regime: Under misspecification MLE converges to the KL-closest member of the family, which may still be badly wrong for the quantity of interest; with latent variables the likelihood is nonconcave and EM finds only local optima (Section 24.4).

layer2.mapping: Probability calibration in the engine is likelihood-based: distributions over game outcomes are fitted by maximizing log likelihood on settled games, which is the same operation as minimizing log-loss, so calibration quality and probabilistic accuracy are one measurement, not two.
layer2.telemetry: Log likelihood (equivalently log-loss) per probabilistic model on settled games, tracked over time to detect drift.

primitives.name: Rademacher complexity: the expected ability of a class to fit random sign noise measures its effective size and bounds the generalization gap
primitives.verbatim_quote: Then, the Rademacher complexity of F with respect to S is defined as follows:

symbol_and_unit_ledger.F o S: the set of evaluation vectors (f(z_1), ..., f(z_m)) as f ranges over F
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Lemma 26.2: expected representativeness of S is at most twice the expected Rademacher complexity

assumptions: The measure is data-dependent: it is computed on the actual sample, unlike VC-dimension
Talagrand contraction and the Rademacher calculus (Section 26.1.1) let it be bounded for composite classes
primitives.breakdown_regime: Estimating Rademacher complexity for rich classes is itself computationally hard, and expectation-over-sigma bounds hide tail behavior; for linear classes it reduces to norm quantities (Section 26.2) which is where it is most usable.

layer2.mapping: The engine's capacity audits are Rademacher in spirit: a candidate model class is stress-tested by its ability to fit randomized labels on the same historical features. A class that can fit noise gets a complexity charge proportional to that ability before its real-label performance is believed.
layer2.telemetry: Noise-fitting scores per model class: best achievable fit to permuted or random labels on historical feature matrices.

primitives.name: PAC-Bayes bound: a posterior over hypotheses generalizes according to its empirical risk plus the KL divergence from a data-independent prior
primitives.verbatim_quote: theorem 31.1 Let D be an arbitrary distribution over an example domain Z. Let H be a hypothesis class and let ` : H × Z → [0, 1] be a loss function.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Q: posterior distribution over H, may depend on the sample S
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P: prior distribution over H, fixed before seeing S
symbol_and_unit_ledger.L_D(Q), L_S(Q): expected risk of a hypothesis drawn from Q, true and empirical

assumptions: Loss bounded in [0, 1]
The bound holds simultaneously for all posteriors Q with probability at least 1 - delta over S
primitives.breakdown_regime: A poorly matched prior makes the KL term huge and the bound vacuous; the bound controls the average hypothesis under Q, so extracting one deterministic hypothesis needs an extra derandomization step.

layer2.mapping: The engine maintains explicit prior weights over signal families (from theory and past seasons) and updates them into posteriors as games settle; the PAC-Bayes form prices that updating: families whose posteriors move far from prior must show proportionally more empirical success, which is implemented as a shrinkage rule on family weights.
layer2.telemetry: Prior and posterior weight vectors per family at each update, with the KL divergence between them reported alongside performance.

reasoning_traces.think: This book is the disciplined core underneath almost every machine learning method the engine will ever use, and its architecture is itself a primitive: it separates the question of what learning is from the question of which algorithm to run, and it refuses to discuss an algorithm until the statistical contract it must satisfy has been stated. The statistical learning framework fixes the objects: an unknown distribution, a sample, a hypothesis class chosen before the data arrives, a loss, and two risks, the true risk that matters and the empirical risk that can be computed. Everything else in the book is an account of the gap between those two risks and of the levers that control it. ERM is the naive bridge across the gap, and the memorization example shows the bridge collapsing when the class is too rich for the sample. The repairs come in families. Restrict the class and charge for its size, which yields finite-class bounds, VC-dimension, and the fundamental theorem that makes finite VC-dimension the exact boundary of learnability for binary classification. Reorder the class by prior preference and pay per hypothesis rather than per class, which yields SRM, MDL, and the Occam bound in which description length is literally a currency that buys generalization. Change the loss so the optimization becomes convex, which yields surrogate losses, hinge, logistic-style objectives, and the whole convex learning apparatus with its Lipschitz and smoothness bookkeeping. Stabilize the algorithm so that one example cannot move the output much, which yields the exact identity equating the generalization gap to replace-one instability and explains why Tikhonov regularization works. Optimize with noisy gradients and averaging, which yields SGD with the B rho over root T rate that prices accuracy in iterations. Exploit geometry, which yields margins, Hard and Soft SVM, and the equivalence showing that margin maximization is norm regularization in disguise. Exploit algebra, which yields the kernel trick and similarity-based reasoning over implicitly infinite feature spaces. Then the book changes the contract itself three more times: validation, where a fresh sample buys an algorithm-independent estimate; online learning, where there is no distribution at all and regret against the best fixed expert replaces risk; and the Bayesian-flavored contracts, MLE for generative models and PAC-Bayes, where a distribution over hypotheses is the output and KL divergence to a prior is the complexity charge. Rademacher complexity closes the loop by making capacity measurable on the actual sample, including the devastating diagnostic of fitting random signs. For a reasoning engine, the transferable content is not any single algorithm but the discipline that every performance claim decomposes into a fit term and a complexity or stability term, that every selection procedure consumes the data it selects on, and that every guarantee names its assumptions: i.i.d. sampling, bounded loss, separability, convexity, a prior fixed in advance. A component that cannot state its term in this decomposition is not yet understood, whatever its backtest says. The book also teaches the failure taxonomy: overfitting is capacity outrunning sample; underfitting is approximation error that no sample size repairs; instability is a generalization gap with a mechanical cause; and a vacuous bound is information, because it marks exactly where intuition is running ahead of evidence. The middle chapters fill in the menagerie that these principles govern, and each entry is a different trade among the same quantities. Linear predictors are the laboratory: halfspaces are learned by linear programming or by the Perceptron, whose mistake bound already contains the margin idea in embryo, since it depends on the ratio between data radius and separator norm rather than on dimension. Least squares is ERM with a closed form, logistic regression is ERM with a smooth probabilistic surrogate, and both show how the choice of loss quietly redefines the problem being solved. Boosting answers a question posed purely inside the theory, whether weak and strong learnability coincide, and answers it with an algorithm whose reweighting scheme doubles as a margin maximizer, which is why its generalization analysis runs through the same norm-and-margin quantities as SVMs. Decision trees and nearest neighbor mark the nonparametric edge: trees buy interpretability with greedy gain heuristics and pruning as their complexity control, while nearest neighbor carries the curse of dimensionality as its estimation error made geometric, a reminder that some classes have sample complexity exponential in the dimension no matter how they are fit. Neural networks are treated with unusual honesty: their expressive power is easy to demonstrate, their sample complexity is boundable through the same capacity tools, but the runtime of learning them is where the guarantees stop, and SGD with backpropagation is presented as the practical engine whose success the theory only partially explains. The unsupervised chapters extend the contract rather than escaping it: clustering is shown to have no assumption-free foundation at all, with impossibility results forcing the practitioner to state an objective, k-means being the canonical cost whose optimization is NP-hard even though its Lloyd-style heuristic is trivial; dimensionality reduction is compression with a stated distortion budget, PCA keeping variance, random projections keeping distances by the Johnson-Lindenstrauss phenomenon, and compressed sensing recovering sparse signals from few measurements, three different priors about where the information lives. Generative models close the algorithmic arc by reversing the direction of modeling: instead of a boundary, fit a distribution, by maximum likelihood when the model is fully observed and by the EM alternation when latent variables hide part of it, with Naive Bayes and LDA as the tractable special cases. Part IV then sharpens the measuring instruments themselves: Rademacher calculus for composite classes, covering numbers and chaining for turning metric structure into bounds, the full proof of the fundamental theorem, the Natarajan dimension carrying the VC characterization into multiclass problems, compression bounds showing that any hypothesis reconstructible from a small subsample inherits a guarantee, and PAC-Bayes making the prior-to-posterior movement itself the priced quantity. Even the appendices are load-bearing: the concentration inequalities in Appendix B are the single probabilistic engine inside nearly every proof in the book, the reason sample sizes so often appear inside square roots and logarithms. Read whole, the book's unity is that learnability is never a property of an algorithm alone; it is a relation among a class, a loss, a sample size, a computational budget, and a stated prior, and changing any one of the five silently changes the claim.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from Valiant's 1984 PAC model and Vapnik and Chervonenkis's capacity theory through the 1990s synthesis of statistical learning theory, with Boosting born from the theoretical question of whether weak and strong learnability coincide (Kearns and Valiant's question, answered by Schapire and Freund), SVMs from Vapnik's school, stability from Bousquet and Elisseeff, Rademacher complexity from Koltchinskii and Panchenko, and PAC-Bayes from McAllester. Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, both formed inside that tradition, reorganized it into a single textbook in 2014, which is why the book reads as a genealogy made rigorous: each chapter's machinery is presented as the repair of the previous chapter's failure mode.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors model their reader as someone who will be tempted by algorithms first and guarantees later, and they write against that temptation on every page: definitions precede methods, counterexamples precede fixes, and every success is stated with its assumptions attached. Their model of the domain is austere and adversarial: distributions are arbitrary, samples can mislead, and a claim is only as good as its worst case, yet the book is constructive throughout, because each impossibility result (No-Free-Lunch, NP-hardness of ERM for 0-1 loss) is immediately converted into a design instruction about what prior structure or surrogate objective to adopt instead.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in this book veto practices that other layers of a system find attractive. Uniform convergence vetoes reporting the winner's backtest without charging for the size of the pool it was selected from. The validation theorem vetoes reusing a selection set as an estimation set. The stability identity vetoes trusting any model whose output swings when one training example changes, regardless of its average accuracy. No-Free-Lunch vetoes any claim of a universally best method, and the error decomposition vetoes prescribing more data for a problem that is actually approximation error, or a richer class for a problem that is actually estimation error. These vetoes bind every other signal layer.

universal_lens: Read as a general template, the book says: any system that learns from samples must declare its hypothesis space before seeing data, must price every claim by the gap between what it can measure (empirical performance) and what it cares about (true performance), and must pay for capacity, instability, and prior mismatch in a stated currency, whether that currency is log class size, VC-dimension, description length, norm, margin, or KL divergence. The currencies are interchangeable views of one quantity: how much of the sample's information a hypothesis consumed.
gsi_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Institute, this book is the curriculum spine for teaching rigorous model evaluation: it supplies the vocabulary (risk, capacity, stability, regret) and the canonical counterexamples (memorization, No-Free-Lunch) that let students audit any sports model, including the Institute's own, by asking which term of the error decomposition a claimed improvement actually reduces and what evidence would distinguish the terms.
gse_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Edge engine, this book supplies the operating law of the reasoning layer: signals are hypotheses in declared classes, backtests are empirical risks that must be charged uniform-convergence and selection penalties before promotion, model combination follows SRM, RLM, and Weighted-Majority forms with explicit penalties and weights, margins and stability audits gate confidence, and live performance is tracked as regret against fixed benchmarks. Every promotion, demotion, and retirement decision in the engine can be written in this book's vocabulary and audited against its theorems.
